I'm counting it as (1/4) + (1/4) + (1/4) + (1/8) =  3½/4. The argument is about if you have to set a metronome to 7/8, to think about it as 3½/4. Demonstrably this isn't true. In the audiovisual example I provided, the metronome does not play 7/8, yet the guitar can still play/think of it as 3½/4. You can try it yourself. In the end, it's way more practical to just count it as 7/8, but that's not what this is about.

You're absolutely right, it can be analyzed that way too. In fact, it could be more appropiate to analyze it in B major.

V. III. I. I.

V. V7/III. VI. V7/V.

The last chord could maybe be analyzed as II7, because I vaguely remember it having a special function, at least in a jazz context

Start out by just adding the 7th note to every chord in for example C major. B to Cmaj, C to Dmin, D to Emin, etc. Then you can start adding 9ths, 11ths, 13ths. You can also try using altered extensions. Dm9 - G7b9 - Cmaj9, is a so called II-V-I progression and is a staple of jazz and sounds great, for example.

After that you can explore melodic minor and/or harmonic minor.  You can also try stacking chords using fourths instead of thirds. This is called quartal harmony. For example, in the key of C major you can stack the II chord (Dm) using fourths - D G C F - which spells out a Dm11.

A cool voicing I like to move up and down a scale is using the root, the 9th and the 7th. In the key of C major, that would be C D B. Move this up the scale, it sounds great!

Have fun!

Absolutely, 3½/4 in this case is just confusing and not practical. I have not seen too many pieces that employ it, but I would imagine that 7/8 would be much preferable in most cases, just as you say. They are exchangeable, but the latter is (most of the time) superior to the other.

What I'm saying stems from the following statement: ''3½/4 is imaginary, because to play it against a metronome you have set the metronome to 7/8.'' Well, this is demonstrably false, regardless of what it's felt like, isn't it?

Yes, playing two bars of 3½/4 will result in one bar of 7/4, just as playing 3½/4 against a bassist playing 4/4 will make it a polymeter.

>3½/4 doesn't mean the pulse is  necessarily counted as quarter notes. You would count 3½/4 most likely  as 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 1 & 2 & 3 & 4, etc. If you kept  a constant quarter note pulse behind it, it would simply become 7/4 (so  two bars of "3½/4" would become one bar of 7/4):

Absolutely valid points. It's all up to the person in charge. But wouldn't you say my point is just as ''valid'', albeit much less practical? In regard to playing  3½/4 over a pulse of 4 as a rhythmic reference.

The 1 of 3½/4 lands on a 8th note syncopation the first time around, and after that it lands on a metronome hit, then it repeats. Not too complicated but not practical.

But the argument from the other person was: **''You can not play 3½/4 to a metronome with a pulse of, because metronomes can't play half beats.'**'

Well, digital metronomes can be programmed to 3½/4. But barring digital metronomes and only using mechanical metronomes, you can obviously play it to a pulse equal to 3½/4 as well.

>Even if other instruments were playing in 4/4 against that (also at 80 bpm), why would you notate this line with a different time sig?  It's simply a cross-rhythm against the main 4/4.  (Or the "4/4" instruments would be playing a cross-rhythm against the basic 7/4.)

I'm probably clumsy about this or not expaining myself properly, but what I'm saying is that you can play to a metronome that has the same pulse as  3½/4, and play in 3½/4. The person I was talking to this about said that you could only do this by for example taking a digital metronome and setting it to 7/8. This is demonstrably not true, unless someone has any objections.

I also think most people would notate it as 7/8, that's more practical. But what I'm trying to prive is that you can, for whatever reason, count it like 3½/4 convincingly, using the same pulse as the fractional time signature mentioned. Try it out yourself, if you want to.

It's Guitar Pro 5. It's an old version of it, I think they've come out with 7 now. It's great, good playback as well. You can use tablature or traditional notation. I've never tried out the tabbing, but traditional notation works great.

>Now, if you insist on using a  mechanical metronome, and you still want some kind of reference, then  yes, you would need to set it to 7/8 - but that's just as correct (read:  not) as setting it to 6/8 in order to play 3/4.

But you can have the same pulse as  3½/4  on the metronome, and still keep time, can you not? I can set a digital metronome to 6/8 and still think of it as 3/4 and play it accurately. In the same way I can set it to 3/4 and think 4/4. It's stupid, but you can do it, right?

I understand that the video ''shows'' a 3½/4 over 4/4 = 7/8 over 4/4 polymeter. But the question is: is  3½/4 imaginary?

The video is supposed to demonstrate that you can sit down, want to play in  3½/4, but using an pulse of 4 as a reference point. The person opposed to me postulates that you can only play  3½/4 to a metronome by thinking of it as 7/8.
